The traffic management system in Odisha’s capital city broke down once again today, leaving hundreds of commuters stranded in a massive gridlock that stretched from Hanspal to Vani Vihar.
The prolonged delay caused severe hardship for daily travellers enduring scorching heat, while even emergency services were hit as an ambulance remained stuck in the standstill traffic.
The root cause of the chaos has been traced to a severe bottleneck near Palasuni, where a 6-lane stretch compresses abruptly into just 2 lanes. The sudden reduction in road capacity, combined with a total lack of traffic regulation on-site, turned the major highway artery into a crawling parking lot.
Adding fuel to the fire is the unrestricted movement of heavy goods vehicles and trucks through the city core during peak hours. Unlike other major urban centres across the country, where strict ‘No-Entry’ hours are enforced for heavy vehicles to prevent congestion, Bhubaneswar currently lacks effective restrictions.
The situation has triggered widespread public outrage against administrative apathy. Commuters have questioned why local authorities have failed to implement standard heavy-vehicle restrictions and proper lane management systems at key bottlenecks. Until structural fixes and traffic regulations are put into practice, everyday travellers in the capital continue to pay the price.

Mr Williams said: “Drivers’ strong feelings about the poor quality of the UK’s roads are a reflection both of a long-term lack of investment in road maintenance and repair by local authorities, and of the road surface issues exacerbated by a particularly wet winter, and now an extremely hot summer.
“Fortunately, the Government has increased its efforts to address the problem.
“Council highway budgets in England have been increased to a record £1.6bn for 2025-26 and in November’s budget, £7.3bn was allocated for road improvement works between now and the end of the decade which will allow councils to make long-term maintenance plans.”
Mike Hansford, the chief executive of the Road Surface Treatments Association, said owing to extremes in the UK weather, “it’s more important than ever to ensure our roads are made more resilient for the future through application of early life, preventative treatments”.
He added: “The industry has responded to these extremes in our weather, through further modification of the binders used in these treatments, which makes them more resistant to both summer and winter extreme temperatures.”
The Department for Transport issued new reporting requirements for English councils in June which require them to prove they are doing more to fix potholes and future-proof roads.
This is aimed at encouraging full resurfacing of roads rather than short-term fixes.
Local authorities risk losing up to a third of their funding for road maintenance if they fail to demonstrate they are working effectively.

Extreme heat's multiple pathways
Unlike many natural hazards, extreme heat does not operate through a single pathway. It places additional stress on energy systems, increases the likelihood of power outages, damages transport infrastructure, affects water availability and raises bushfire risk. It can disrupt business operations, increase workers' compensation claims, affect agricultural productivity and place growing pressure on health systems.
